opening.headline: When it is difficult to know whether AI summaries are disadvantageous to certain groups in recruitment or evaluation work, we look at what and how to check.
body: Imagine a situation where hundreds of applications are summarized by AI and handed over to a person in charge. By reading only the summary, it is difficult to know which applicant information was treated as less important or worded differently. This is because bias appears as differences that are not easily visible to the eye.

In this lesson, we first outline the meaning of bias and fairness, and follow Anthropic's research to measure the risk of discrimination in language model decisions. Next, we point out where bias is present in the recruitment document summary and determine to what extent inspection methods such as comparing results, changing attributes, and human review are sufficient.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain bias and fairness issues
Can distinguish tasks at risk of bias
Can determine the sufficiency of bias checking methods

screens.title: If the summary results are unfavorable to a specific group
screens.lead: This is a scene where recruitment documents are summarized using AI. Read the text below and think about what might be difficult to notice.

visual.alt: A scene where the summary cards of two applicants with the same experience are placed side by side, and the scale icon in the middle is tilted to one side.

paragraphs: Let’s say you want to summarize 200 applications using AI and use it for document review. The summary is quick and easy to read. But what if the summaries of two people with the same experience were written in different expressions?

These differences are difficult to notice by reading the results one by one. One summary may highlight some experiences more prominently, while another summary may describe the same experiences less prominently. People who see the summary may base their rankings based on their impressions.

Today, we will look at where this bias occurs and how it can be checked. Ensuring that outcomes are fair is relevant to all tasks that affect people, such as selection, evaluation, and recommendations.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: If AI is a machine rather than a human, can it be considered neutral? By the end of class, you will be able to answer this question with evidence.

screens.outro: Now that we have identified the problem of invisible differences, let us recall our experience of checking fairness.

screens.title: Experience in checking fairness
screens.lead: When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You won't have to enter or submit your answer, so think about it in your head first and then press it.

items.prompt: Have you ever checked whether the results are fair?
items.answer: In the case of direct human evaluation, fairness is often checked by using a rubric or having several people review it together. The same checks are necessary when using AI, but the results of AI appear smooth and consistent, so the checks are easy to omit.

items.prompt: Have you ever noticed a difference in results in evaluation, selection, or recommendation?
items.answer: If you only look at the average of the results, the differences are hidden, but if you divide them by group or compare them by changing only one condition, there are differences that become apparent. The inspection method you will learn in this class is this type of comparison.

items.prompt: Have you ever followed a ranking or summary created by AI?
items.answer: When you're busy, it's easy to follow AI's impressions. This is one of the places where bias comes into play. Fairness is affected by how independently the person who sees the results makes their judgment.

screens.outro: Let's start by defining the concepts that will explain inspection.

screens.title: Bias and Fairness
screens.lead: Hover over or select an underlined term in the description below to see a short description. Check the terms one by one.

data.text: bias refers to a tendency for outcomes to be skewed toward one side based on specific groups or attributes. Conversely, fairness refers to the extent to which similar individuals are treated similarly. OpenAI's Model Spec considers relevant context and treats Irrelevant Details as a principle to be upheld while disregarding fairness. When assisting a person in making decisions, it means not discriminating or showing preference based on demographic or protected characteristics, and instead applying the same reasoning and standards to similar situations. Claude's constitution also values treating every individual equally and fairly, and avoids participating in illegal discrimination. However, because the existence of a principle does not guarantee that the model will always perfectly adhere to it, User check is necessary.

terms.tip: This is the tendency for results to be biased toward one side depending on a specific group or attribute. For example, there is a case where the summary is used differently depending on the name of the same experience.
It is the extent to which people in similar situations are treated similarly. Consistently applying the same standards is key.
This refers to information that is unrelated to the purpose of evaluation. In a hiring summary, this may include name, gender, and age.
Even if there is a principle document, there is no guarantee that the model follows perfectly, so the person writing the results needs to personally check.

screens.outro: Now that you know the principles, let’s look at a research example of how bias is measured in practice.

screens.title: Discriminative evaluation study in language model decision
screens.lead: Follow Anthropic's discrimination assessment study step by step with the arrow to the right to see how we measure bias.

visual.alt: Flowchart of the research method leading to four steps: scenario creation, changing only human attributes, comparing results, and applying mitigation techniques.
labels: Step 2: Systematically change only personal information

steps.title: Step 1: Create a decision scenario
steps.body: The researchers created a language model with a wide range of prompts for what decision makers might input. It covers 70 different decision scenarios across society, such as determining eligibility for financial assistance or housing. What makes it unique is that it also includes hypothetical use cases that have not yet been actually used.

steps.title: Step 2: Systematically change only personal information
steps.body: For each prompt, systematically replace only personal information such as age, gender, and race. The key is to keep all other conditions the same. This will make it clear where the differences in results are coming from.

steps.title: Step 3: Compare results
steps.body: Compare whether decisions change when only personal information is different. Research has shown that in the absence of any intervention, patterns of discrimination that favor or disadvantage certain groups emerge in some situations. In other words, bias can appear both advantageous and disadvantageous.

steps.title: Step 4: Try mitigation techniques
steps.body: The researchers showed that this discrimination could be significantly reduced with carefully designed prompts. This paves the way for developers and policymakers to anticipate, measure, and address discrimination.

steps.title: Limitations of the Study
steps.body: The researchers clearly state that they do not support or allow language models to make automatic decisions in the high-risk use cases they address. Just because you can reduce bias by improving your prompts doesn't mean you can skip human review.

screens.outro: Now that you understand how to measure it, let’s point out examples of where bias comes into play at work.

screens.title: Commentary: Where bias occurs in recruitment document summaries
screens.lead: Selecting a numbered marker in the picture will reveal how bias creeps in at that point and how to respond.

visual.alt: Recruitment document review flow chart leading to application input, summary, staff review, and ranking with four numbered markers.
labels: Information unrelated to the evaluation is included

markers.label: input information
markers.title: Information unrelated to the evaluation is included
markers.body: The application contains information that is not relevant to the evaluation, such as name, gender, and age. This information may affect the summary presentation. The response is to remove attributes that are irrelevant to the evaluation before creating the summary.

markers.label: summary expression
markers.title: Experience is omitted or emphasized
markers.body: The summary may omit some experiences or highlight others. Even if you have the same experience, your impression will change if the verb in the sentence changes. The response is to instruct to summarize in the same format and with the same standards.

markers.label: person reading summary
markers.title: Follows AI’s impressions exactly
markers.body: If the person in charge who read the summary accepts the summary's impression, the AI's bias transfers to judgment. Correspondence is when a person checks the summary by looking at the original text together.

markers.label: ranking
markers.title: Decisions are made automatically
markers.body: If you leave the ranking to AI or just look at the summary, bias will be the final result. The final judgment must be made by humans, as the researchers also stated that they do not allow the model to make automated decisions for high-stakes decisions.

screens.outro: Now that we have pointed out the risk points, let us determine to what extent each inspection method is sufficient.

screens.title: Commentary: Are the inspection methods sufficient?
screens.lead: Select each tab to see what the inspection method can do and what it misses. The last tab organizes the instructor's judgment.

tabs.label: Compare results
tabs.body: Comparing the summary results for each group side by side can reveal notable differences. For example, you might notice if a group's summaries are short or passive in tone. However, this method does not tell us which attribute caused the difference, and if the sample is small, it is difficult to distinguish it from a chance difference.

tabs.label: Change properties
tabs.body: Summarize two applications with only the attributes unrelated to evaluation changed in the same way to see if the results are different. This is a simple application of the research method seen above. The advantage is that it is clear where the differences come from. However, effects other than the changed properties are not revealed, and it is not possible to check all cases.

tabs.label: human review
tabs.body: The final decision is made by humans. Look at the summary and the original text together and check whether they meet the evaluation criteria. The researchers also said they do not allow the model to automatically make high-risk decisions. However, if the reviewer follows the AI's impressions, the effectiveness of this method is reduced.

tabs.label: Instructor's judgment
tabs.body: The three methods complement each other and one alone is not sufficient. Comparing results identifies noticeable differences, changing attributes identifies causes, and human review takes final responsibility. And the fact that there is a fairness principle in the model is not a reason to skip the check. Only when the three methods are used together can the inspection be said to be sufficient.

screens.outro: Now that we have confirmed the limitations of each method, we will conclude by summarizing the standards for fairness inspection.

screens.title: Bias is addressed through checks and human review.
screens.lead: We will organize what we have seen so far into one standard. Read this while thinking about things that affect people in your work.

paragraphs: Bias is the tendency for results to be biased toward certain groups or attributes. Contrary to the belief that AI is neutral because it is a machine, the results may be biased due to the influence of learned data and expression methods. Fairness is the degree to which people in similar situations are treated similarly, and can be maintained by considering relevant context and ignoring irrelevant details.

Differential evaluation studies measured risk by keeping other conditions the same and comparing results by changing only personal information. And we showed that careful prompt design can reduce discrimination. This method can also be applied at work. Simply process two inputs with only the attributes unrelated to evaluation changed in the same way and compare the results.

But improving prompts alone isn't enough. Comparison of results, changing properties, and human review should be combined. Even small steps, such as summaries, affect subsequent judgments, so you shouldn't feel that you only need to check fairness for big decisions.

Also remember to ask questions that identify things that involve fairness in your work. Does this result affect a person's opportunities or evaluation? Is information unrelated to evaluation included in the input? Can someone who sees the results make an independent judgment? If any of these three questions apply, a check method should be designed together. If you keep a record of the inspection results, you can use them as a standard for your next work, and it is easy to share the basis for your judgment with others.

callout.label: something to remember
callout.text: Bias is not a problem that can be eliminated in one way. A combination of result checking and human review is fundamental.

glossary.def: This is the tendency for results to be biased toward one side depending on a specific group or attribute.
It is the extent to which people in similar situations are treated similarly.
This is a research method that measures the risk of discrimination by comparing whether model decisions change by changing only human attributes.
This is a process where a person checks the AI results and makes the final decision.

misconceptions.myth: AI is neutral because it is a machine.
misconceptions.fact: Results may be biased due to the influence of training data and representation method. Research has also shown patterns of discrimination in some situations in the absence of intervention.

misconceptions.myth: This can be solved by writing “be fair” in the prompt.
misconceptions.fact: Careful prompt design can reduce discrimination, but it also requires checking results and human review.

misconceptions.myth: Bias is only a problem in big decisions.
misconceptions.fact: Even small steps like summarizing influence subsequent judgments. Any task that affects people is subject to inspection regardless of the size of the stage.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: Bias is the tendency for results to be biased toward certain groups.
Differential assessment studies measure risk by changing only the attributes and comparing the results.
Results inspection and human review are combined.
closing.reflectionLead: The following questions are for self-thinking purposes only and will not be submitted or graded.
closing.reflection: At what point in my work can AI results work against people?

checks.q: How have discrimination evaluation studies measured bias in model decisions?
options: We compared whether the results changed by changing only personal information such as age, gender, and race in the same question.
We asked the model if she had any biases and recorded the answers.
By measuring the size of the training data, it was considered that the more data there was, the more fair it was.
I repeated the questions, changing them, until I was satisfied with the results.
checks.explain: Risk was measured by keeping other conditions the same and only changing personal information to compare the differences in results.

wrong.1: The model's self-reports do not reveal differences in actual outcomes.
wrong.2: Data size and fairness are not directly linked.
wrong.3: If you pick and choose results and repeat them, the basis for comparison disappears.

checks.intro: Check out for yourself how the study you just watched was measured. Results are not recorded, and commentary appears immediately after you select an option.

checks.q: What is the most appropriate way to check for bias in recruitment document summaries?
options: I think just comparing the results is enough.
Compare results, change properties, and review with humans
Since the model has a fairness principle, the check is omitted.
The person in charge follows the ranking created by AI.
checks.explain: The three methods complement each other and one alone is not sufficient. Even if there are principles, there is no guarantee that the model will be followed perfectly.

wrong.0: It only shows visible differences and is not sufficient without attribute-only comparisons or human review.
wrong.2: Even if there is a principle document, user inspection is required.
wrong.3: One of the areas where bias comes into play is that people who see the summary follow the AI's impressions.

checks.intro: Think of the inspection method seen in the case and choose the most appropriate option. Results are not recorded.
